steelman: Past a small agent count, adding specialists reverses sign because the dominant cost is cross-agent contamination, not tokens. Under a flat-context orchestrator, steering accuracy collapses from 60% at N=3 to 21% at N=10 as one agent's instructions leak into another's decisions, a mechanism named context pollution [s1]; this is an attention-and-isolation failure that a bigger model does not fix. An independent cost-accuracy benchmark corroborates that coordination gets worse as designs grow more elaborate, with inter-agent coordination failures climbing from 8.1% (parallel) to 12.4% (hierarchical) to 14.2% (reflexive), and the top-scoring reflexive design costing 2.30x the sequential baseline [s2]. Crucially, the same benchmark shows a structured hierarchical design recovering 98.5% of the best F1 (0.929 vs 0.943) at 60.7% of the cost ($0.261 vs $0.430) [s2], so a scoped or hierarchical alternative beats a flat swarm and 'add another agent' should require evidence rather than be the default.
strongest_attack: The two pillars measure different things and neither cleanly isolates agent COUNT as the causal lever. s1's 60% to 21% is a steering-accuracy metric on a flat-context orchestrator [s1], not task success, and it demonstrates that FLAT context degrades with scale, not that multi-agent per se is bad; context pollution could be an artifact of the flat design rather than of adding agents. s2's climb from 8.1% to 14.2% is indexed by architecture TYPE (parallel, hierarchical, reflexive), not by number of agents, so the coordination-failure trend is confounded with design style [s2]. Worse for a blanket 'more agents bad' reading, s2's headline positive result cuts the other way: the multi-agent reflexive design still wins on accuracy (F1 0.943) and the multi-agent hierarchical design captures 98.5% of that at 60.7% of the cost [s2], which shows that structured multi-agent designs pay off. Stitching a steering metric from one paper and task-level F1/cost from another (different datasets and tasks) to assert a single 'sign flip past three or four agents' is apples-to-oranges.
reconciliation: The thesis survives, largely because it is already hedged to exactly the target the attack leaves standing. It does not claim multi-agent is bad; it claims the FLAT-swarm reflex has the sign backwards past three or four agents and that a scoped or hierarchical design wins. s1's collapse from 60% to 21% is explicitly a property of a flat-context orchestrator [s1], which is the flat swarm the thesis indicts, so 'artifact of flat context' is the thesis's point, not a refutation. The hierarchical 98.5%-at-60.7% result [s2] reinforces rather than refutes the claim: structure recovers most accuracy at roughly 60% of cost, which is precisely the so-what. What does NOT survive is any strong causal claim keyed to raw agent count: s2 varies architecture type, not N, so 'coordination overhead compounds with agent count' must weaken to 'coordination failure rises with orchestration elaborateness' [s2]. The cross-paper stitching also forces a narrower phrasing (two independent signals pointing the same direction, not one measured curve).
strengthened_argument: For flat-context orchestration, steering accuracy degrades sharply with scale (60% at N=3 to 21% at N=10) via context pollution, an isolation failure a bigger model does not address [s1]; and across architectures, coordination failure and cost both rise with orchestration elaborateness, the reflexive design costing 2.30x the sequential baseline [s2]. Therefore the flat-swarm default is dominated: a structured hierarchical design recovers 98.5% of the best accuracy (F1 0.929 vs 0.943) at 60.7% of the cost ($0.261 vs $0.430) [s2]. The defensible claim is not 'more agents always hurt' but 'flat, unscoped scaling hurts, so isolation and structure, not agent count or model size, are the lever, and adding an agent should require evidence it beats a scoped or hierarchical baseline.'
reason: The core claim is non-trivial and falsifiable (it predicts flat orchestration degrades with scale while scoped/hierarchical designs recover most accuracy at lower cost), and it survives the strongest attack because its hedges pre-concede exactly what the evidence cannot support: s1 measures the flat-context failure the thesis targets [s1], and s2's hierarchical-at-60.7% result actively confirms the 'structure beats swarm' so-what [s2]. It stays defensible only in the strengthened form that drops any raw agent-count causality (s2 varies architecture type, not N) and treats the two papers as independent corroborating signals rather than one continuous curve.
